reference.source: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours
clinicalPearls: Highly aggressive, poorly differentiated epithelial malignancy of the sinonasal tract that is distinct from squamous cell and neuroendocrine carcinomas.
Typically presents with a short history and rapidly progressive nasal obstruction, epistaxis, facial pain, proptosis, diplopia and cranial neuropathies.
Usually bulky at diagnosis with extensive invasion of the orbit, skull base and anterior cranial fossa.
It is largely a diagnosis of exclusion requiring immunohistochemistry to rule out NUT carcinoma, SMARCB1-deficient carcinoma, neuroendocrine carcinoma, lymphoma, melanoma and olfactory neuroblastoma.
Tumour cells are pancytokeratin positive, typically negative or only focally positive for neuroendocrine markers, and show no squamous or glandular differentiation.
Retained INI-1 (SMARCB1) helps separate it from SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, and NUT immunostaining excludes NUT carcinoma; an IDH2-mutant subset is increasingly recognised.
Management is multimodal, often induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiotherapy or surgery guided by treatment response and resectability.
Local recurrence and distant metastasis are common, so response-adapted therapy and close surveillance are central to care.
reference.pathophysiology: Sinonasal undifferentiated carcinoma is a carcinoma of uncertain histogenesis thought to arise from the Schneiderian mucosa or olfactory epithelium of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses. It is composed of sheets, nests and trabeculae of medium-to-large cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, prominent nucleoli, brisk mitotic activity, frequent tumour necrosis and lymphovascular invasion, and by definition lacks squamous or glandular differentiation. The entity is molecularly heterogeneous, and recognition of related but distinct tumours such as IDH2-mutant carcinoma, NUT carcinoma and SMARCB1-deficient carcinoma has refined its definition as a diagnosis of exclusion.
additionalDifferentials: Sinonasal neuroendocrine or small cell carcinoma
Poorly differentiated or non-keratinising squamous cell carcinoma
additionalInvestigations: Endoscopic biopsy with a broad immunohistochemistry panel (pancytokeratin, p40/p63, synaptophysin, chromogranin, NUT, INI-1/SMARCB1, S100, CD45, HMB-45)
Contrast-enhanced MRI of the sinuses and brain to map dural, orbital and intracranial extension
CT of the sinuses to define bony destruction and skull-base involvement
Molecular testing (IDH2 mutation, NUT rearrangement) to subtype the tumour
Ophthalmology and neurosurgical assessment where orbital or intracranial invasion is present
Serum LDH and lymphoma work-up when lymphoma remains in the differential
redFlags: Rapid tumour growth over weeks with new cranial nerve palsies
Orbital apex or cavernous sinus involvement with visual loss
Intracranial extension with headache and altered mental state
Midface or cheek numbness indicating perineural or skull-base spread
Sudden severe epistaxis from a friable bulky mass
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally poor, with a strong tendency to local recurrence and distant metastasis. Multimodality treatment and a good response to induction chemotherapy are associated with better outcomes, but overall long-term survival remains low.
pitfalls: Labelling a tumour as SNUC without first excluding NUT carcinoma and SMARCB1-deficient carcinoma, which carry different management and prognosis
Under-staging the true intracranial and orbital extent of disease
Managing the tumour as ordinary squamous cell carcinoma
Attributing early nonspecific symptoms to chronic sinusitis and delaying biopsy
Omitting distant staging before committing to an aggressive local treatment plan
references: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours
Cummings Otolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines: Head and Neck Cancers
management: Multimodality treatment planned upfront, typically beginning with platinum-based induction chemotherapy to assess tumour responsiveness
Response-adapted consolidation with concurrent chemoradiotherapy for responders, or craniofacial or endoscopic skull-base resection with adjuvant chemoradiotherapy in selected resectable cases
Management of orbital and intracranial extension in conjunction with ophthalmology and neurosurgery, including reconstruction
Supportive oncological care with nutritional support, pain control and management of treatment toxicity
Surveillance for local recurrence and distant metastasis with clinical review and cross-sectional imaging
Coordinated head-and-neck oncology multidisciplinary planning of treatment sequencing, with consideration of clinical trials
